title: Rediscovering New Orleans clarinet in San Francisco
summary: Back in the US he rebuilt his style, helped by San Francisco Bay Area players and a good banjo and rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: It wasn't until you came around here, was it, that you tried to not restore, but find that New Orleans element in your clarinet. Well, yes.

When I came back, I had to do a lot of things. And I never did want to listen too much at record to copy anybody first, because I realized I can't do what they do, as I mentioned before. Yeah. So what I had to do was close my eyes and picture all those famous guys, especially as I've worked with Frank Matthew for a long time. And I knew how he played, and I still couldn't picture, you know, dogs when I heard him and hear different clarinet players from New Orleans that even wasn't known. And I had to picture all that, you know. Concentrate. And I had to really change my style here to get into jazz. Yeah.

Well, these guys like, these guys like Milky, I think, escaped Frank what so many old fake cats have done. Milky seems to play a more, shall we say, more real, earthy trombones, the real thing, because he isn't imitating. You understand? Yes. He's playing the New Orleans idiom, but he's not imitating.
Yes. That's, that has, that has helped me a lot. Yeah. Him and, and, and Patton.

PT. It's almost like listening to the real thing, don't you hear them? Yes. That, they have, have a lot, very, very, they have a lot of great help. And, and with this guy on banjo, Jack Dick Armstrong, if you have it, it's easy, it makes it so easy for you to play. Yeah. You know, you know, you've got solid rhythm, correct chords, and you don't have to worry.
You know, he's come a long way on banjo, when he first started, he was draggy.
Yeah. Yeah. You know, no more. No. I can get so, I can't play with anybody on banjo, you know.
I like that trio sound anyway, the, about the best of all. Yeah. Yeah, that trio. And then something, with Erickson. Yeah. He's a wild, wild piano player. Yeah.

So, you see the environment, I was lucky to fill in with Bob, and Parkstock, and Erickson, and I was three all the keys, and I was lucky to fill in with them. Yeah. And it helped me a lot, so I'm telling you.
I think Milky could be a great trombonist if you wanted to be.
Yeah, well, he should, I mean, he's good, there's no doubt about it. And if you don't seem to want to put the time...
